title: Tracebility Of Memory
content_html:
Tracebility of memory

If you adopt dependent origination + causal determinism, memory is in principle intact, woven into the causal fabric of the universe. But whether it is traceable depends on perspective: physics suggests information is conserved but practically unrecoverable; Buddhism suggests karmic traces persist but always as dependent, empty, and ever-changing.

Dependent Origination (Buddhism) states that nothing arises independently; every phenomenon depends on causes and conditions. So a memory isn’t a static “thing,” but an event arising from networks of causes (neurons, perceptions, contexts). Each act of remembering is part of a causal chain extending backward, ultimately without a first cause (linked to “emptiness” and “no-self”). In physics, information is conserved (in most formulations), so that even processes that look destructive (e.g. entropy increase, black hole evaporation debates) may preserve information at a fundamental level. If true, then in principle the state of the universe at this moment contains a trace of all past states. Example: In classical physics, the present state determines the past and the future (Laplace’s demon). In quantum physics, it’s subtler (probabilistic, but still governed by unitary evolution).

From a strict causal determinist view: yes, memory (in a broad sense - as trace, imprint, or information) would exist all the way back to the origin of the universe. Each particle’s current state encodes the history of interactions it has had (though scrambled beyond recognition). In Buddhism, this resonates with the idea of “storehouse consciousness” (ālaya-vijñāna) in Yogācāra thought: karmic seeds accumulate and unfold through conditions across lifetimes.

But while information may be conserved, it becomes practically unrecoverable. The universe “remembers,” but the traces are so dispersed and entangled that no agent could reconstruct them. Dependent origination denies an absolute beginning; what we call the “origin” (Big Bang, etc.) is itself conditioned. So “traceable back to the origin” might be more poetic than literal. Memory ≠ exact record: Human memory is constructive and probabilistic, not a cosmic archive. The “cosmic memory” is structural, not experiential.

Lens View of “universal memory”
Physics / Information theory The present state of the universe encodes, in principle, all past states. Information is conserved, though scrambled.
Buddhism / Dependent origination All memories arise in a web of conditions stretching infinitely. Nothing is self-contained; traces of past actions (karma) unfold causally.
Synthesis Memory as a principle is not isolated to brains; it is woven into the fabric of causality itself. Whether reconstructable or not, everything leaves a trace.

Memory is a universal principle of continuity: in physics, as conserved information (though dispersed by entropy); in Buddhism, as karmic and conditional traces (without a first cause).

Conserved but unrecoverable

Physics suggests that nothing is ever truly lost, but the universe hides information so effectively in entropy and chaos that, for all practical purposes, it’s gone - just as human memory can be altered, distorted, or inaccessible even though the traces remain. In Newtonian mechanics, if you know the exact state of the universe (positions + velocities of all particles) at one time, you can calculate both past and future. Nothing is “lost.” Schrödinger’s equation preserves the total information in a wavefunction. Even when events look probabilistic (like particle decay), the full system evolution is deterministic and information-conserving. Hawking once argued that black holes destroy information. Current consensus (holographic principle, AdS/CFT duality) suggests that even here, information is preserved - scrambled on the event horizon and re-emitted, but not erased. So in theory: every event, from the Big Bang onward, leaves a complete informational imprint in the fabric of the universe.

The 2nd law of thermodynamics says systems evolve toward disorder. Information is still there, but dispersed into countless microscopic degrees of freedom. Analogy: Burn a book. Every letter’s arrangement is encoded in the smoke, ash, and photon emissions - but good luck reconstructing the text. Chaotic systems amplify small differences. In principle you could rewind the weather from today’s state, but in practice, the tiniest error explodes exponentially, making reconstruction impossible beyond a short window. Quantum entanglement states that nformation can be hidden in global entangled states, so local observers can’t access the full “record” without impossible measurement precision.

In principle, the universe is like a perfect ledger - every moment encodes the past. In practice, that ledger is written in a code so scrambled, dispersed, and entangled that no being inside the universe could ever read it back. This is why physicists sometimes distinguish “microscopic reversibility” (laws are reversible and conserve information) from “macroscopic irreversibility” (entropy ensures practical forgetting).

The* untraceability of memory* touches both neuroscience and philosophy. Memory is not like replaying a video, each recall is a reconstruction, influenced by context, current state, and expectations. Traces (engrams) are distributed across vast neural networks, in which the exact neurons involved can change over time, making the original “path” unrecoverable. Memories may still exist as latent patterns, but the retrieval pathways decay. They are there, but practically untraceable. As we discussed, the universe doesn’t erase information; it disperses it. Even if every interaction leaves a trace, those traces become so scattered (in photons, molecules, heat dissipation) that reconstructing the original signal is impossible.

Every memory arises conditionally, linked to infinite causes. That very interdependence means no single, isolated “trace” can ever be identified. Memories feel like “mine,” but there is no permanent owner. The sense of a continuous thread is itself a construction. In Yogācāra, karmic seeds persist, but how they unfold cannot be linearly traced - they are conditioned by countless factors.

Memory and Instability

  • Stable record = dead archive. A photograph in a drawer does not change; it can be accessed but never grows.
  • Living memory = unstable reconstruction. Each act of remembering reshapes the trace, mixes in present context, and re-encodes it in altered form.

Instability = plasticity → the condition that allows memory to adapt, integrate new experiences, and remain meaningful. Homeostasis describes how living systems maintain order, but never as frozen stability; instead, they are in constant dynamic balance. Evolution explains how genetic “memory” is unstable - mutations introduce variability, which allows adaptation and survival. At a cellular level, proteins misfold, signals fluctuate; stability emerges only through continual correction and turnover. So instability is not opposed to life - it is the raw material life harnesses.

Entropy: The universe trends toward disorder. Living systems survive by locally resisting entropy through metabolism - using instability as energy source.

Chaotic dynamics: Sensitivity to small changes makes systems unpredictable but also creative (new patterns emerge).

Synthesis:

  • Too stable → dead (unchanging archive, fossilized code).
  • Too unstable → noise (no continuity, only chaos).

Life & memory occupy the middle ground of structured instability. Instability is the condition for adaptability, responsiveness, and meaning. Without it, neither memory nor life could evolve, learn, or change. Instability is not just a flaw to be corrected - it’s the essence of what makes systems alive. Memory, cells, ecosystems, even cultures remain “alive” precisely because they are unstable enough to adapt, yet structured enough not to collapse.

Dissipative structures

Dissipative structures are a key idea from Ilya Prigogine’s work on complexity and thermodynamics. A dissipative structure is an ordered, self-organizing system that exists far from equilibrium by dissipating energy into its environment. They are self-organizing patterns that survive only by consuming energy and exporting entropy. Hurricanes, cells, and even memories fit this logic: they live in flux, not in stasis.

Structure → it shows organization or pattern.
Dissipative → it only persists by consuming energy and exporting entropy.

Closed systems (no energy exchange) tend toward disorder (entropy increases), whereas open systems (with energy and matter flow) can use that flow to build order. The price of local order is increased disorder exported to the environment. A whirlpool in a river: water flow keeps it coherent. Stop the flow, the structure disappears. The whirlpool is “alive” only as long as energy passes through it.

Organisms are dissipative structures - local islands of order made possible by metabolic energy flows. Neural circuits are also dissipative - they need metabolic energy to maintain synaptic plasticity, update, and remain plastic yet stable. The fact that these systems exist only in flux, not as static structures, is what makes them dynamic, adaptive, and “alive.” Prigogine argued that dissipative structures show how order can arise from chaos - instability is not the enemy of organization but its precondition. This links to an earlier point: memory is alive because it is unstable. Both memory and life are dissipative: they rely on instability harnessed by structure.
